key_terms.meaning: A function T: V → W between vector spaces over the same field F with T(u+v) = T(u)+T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u) for all u, v in V and all c in F.
The rule T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v); one of the two conditions that make a map linear.
The rule T(cu) = cT(u) for every scalar c; the second condition for linearity.
A linear map from a vector space V to itself, written T: V → V.
(S ∘ T)(v) = S(T(v)); the composition of two linear maps is again linear.
ker T = {v in V : T(v) = 0}; the set of inputs that land on the zero vector.
Range T = {T(v) : v in V}, a subspace of the codomain W.
nullity T = dim(ker T), the number of independent directions that T destroys.
rank T = dim(Range T), the dimension of the space of outputs.
For T: V → W with V finite-dimensional, dim V = rank T + nullity T.
[T]ᵦᶜ is the matrix whose j-th column holds the coordinates of T(vⱼ) in the basis C.
The matrix P whose columns are the new basis vectors written in the old basis; it converts coordinates between bases.
B = P⁻¹AP for some invertible P; two matrices represent the same operator in different bases exactly when they are similar.
A linear map T that is a bijection and whose inverse T⁻¹ is also linear.
Another name for an invertible linear map; equivalently ker T = {0}.
An invertible linear map; when one exists between V and W, the spaces are called isomorphic, written V ≅ W.
A linear map f: V → F, where F is the field of scalars; the output is a scalar, not a vector.
V* is the vector space of all linear functionals on V, with addition and scalar multiplication defined pointwise.
For a basis {v₁,…,vₙ} of V, the functionals fⁱ with fⁱ(vⱼ) = δᵢⱼ form a basis of V*.

takeaways: Linearity is exactly two checks: T(u+v) = T(u)+T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u); once both hold, T(c₁v₁ + … + cₙvₙ) = c₁T(v₁) + … + cₙT(vₙ) follows free.
The kernel measures what a map destroys and the range measures what it produces; both are subspaces, and T is one-to-one exactly when the kernel is {0}.
The rank-nullity theorem is a conservation law: dimensions of input = dimensions kept as output + dimensions collapsed to zero.
Choosing bases turns an abstract linear map into a concrete matrix, and the columns of that matrix are just the images of the basis vectors written in the target basis.
Changing basis replaces M by P⁻¹MP, so rank, nullity, determinant, trace and eigenvalues are properties of the map, not of the matrix you happened to write down.
A linear map is invertible if and only if it is both one-to-one and onto, and over finite dimensions that is equivalent to rank T = dim V = dim W.
Two finite-dimensional spaces over the same field are isomorphic exactly when they have the same dimension, so every n-dimensional space is a copy of Fⁿ.
A linear functional is a linear map into the field; the dual space V* has the same dimension as V, but its vectors are functionals, not arrows.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always demand three things together — the two-line definition of linearity, a proof or a full statement-and-proof of the rank-nullity theorem, and an explicit matrix built from named bases.

bank.q: Define a linear transformation between vector spaces over a field F. State the two defining conditions and verify from the definition that T(0) = 0 and T(−v) = −T(v) for every linear map T.
outline: State T: V → W with T(u+v) = T(u)+T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u)
Put u = v = 0 to get T(0) = T(0)+T(0), hence T(0) = 0
Put c = −1 and u = v to get T(−v) = −T(v)
Give one linear example (rotation, differentiation, T(x,y) = (x+y, 2x)) and one non-example (T(x) = x²)

bank.q: Define the kernel and the range of a linear map T: V → W. Prove that both are subspaces, and prove that T is one-to-one if and only if ker T = {0}.
outline: Kernel is non-empty since T(0)=0
Closed under addition and scalar multiplication using linearity
Range contains 0 = T(0), closed under addition and scalar multiplication
Injectivity proof: T(u)=T(v) ⟹ T(u−v)=0 ⟹ u−v in ker T; both directions

bank.q: State and prove the rank-nullity (dimension) theorem for a linear map T: V → W with V finite-dimensional.
outline: Let nullity T = k with basis {u₁,…,u_k} of ker T
Extend to a basis {u₁,…,u_k, w₁,…,w_r} of V
Show {T(w₁),…,T(w_r)} spans Range T
Show they are independent using the kernel basis
Conclude rank T = r and dim V = k + r

bank.q: Let T: R³ → R² be T(x, y, z) = (x + 2y, y − z). Find the matrix of T with respect to the standard bases, the kernel, the nullity, the rank, and verify the rank-nullity theorem.
outline: Compute T(e₁), T(e₂), T(e₃) and write them as columns
Solve x + 2y = 0 and y − z = 0 to get ker T = span{(−2, 1, 1)}
nullity T = 1, rank T = 2
Check 3 = 2 + 1

bank.q: Let T: R² → R² have matrix [[2, 1], [0, 3]] in the standard basis. Using the basis B = {(1, 1), (1, 2)}, find the change-of-basis matrix P, compute [T]_B = P⁻¹AP, and verify that the result is similar to A.
outline: Write P with columns (1,1)ᵀ and (1,2)ᵀ
Compute P⁻¹
Multiply P⁻¹AP
State that similarity preserves trace and determinant and check both

bank.q: Prove that a linear map T: V → W is invertible if and only if ker T = {0} and Range T = W, and that the inverse map T⁻¹ is itself linear.
outline: Bijection = injective + surjective
Injectivity equivalent to zero kernel
Show T⁻¹(u+v) = T⁻¹(u) + T⁻¹(v) by applying T to both sides
Show T⁻¹(cu) = cT⁻¹(u) the same way

bank.q: Show that any two finite-dimensional vector spaces over the same field with the same dimension are isomorphic, and use this to decide whether R³ and the space P₂ of polynomials of degree at most 2 are isomorphic.
outline: Choose bases {vᵢ} and {wᵢ}
Define T by T(vᵢ) = wᵢ and extend linearly
Show T is linear, injective (kernel zero) and surjective
Both R³ and P₂ have dimension 3, so they are isomorphic

bank.q: Define a linear functional and the dual space V*. For V = R² with basis {(1,0), (1,1)}, find the dual basis and express the functional f(x, y) = 3x − y in terms of it.
outline: Linear functional: f: V → F linear
V* is a vector space with pointwise operations
Solve f¹(v₁)=1, f¹(v₂)=0 and f²(v₁)=0, f²(v₂)=1
Write f as a linear combination of f¹ and f² and check on the basis vectors

bank.q: For an m × n matrix A, prove that the solution space of the homogeneous system Ax = 0 has dimension n − rank(A), and use this to describe the solutions of a consistent non-homogeneous system Ax = b.
outline: View A as the matrix of a linear map T: Fⁿ → Fᵐ
ker T is exactly the solution set of Ax = 0
Apply rank-nullity: n = rank A + nullity A
General solution = one particular solution + the null space

bank.q: For linear maps S: U → V and T: V → W, prove that T ∘ S is linear, that ker S ⊆ ker(T ∘ S), and that Range(T ∘ S) ⊆ Range T. Show with an example that rank(T ∘ S) can be strictly smaller than both ranks.
outline: Check additivity and homogeneity of the composition
Element-wise inclusion proofs
Example: two nilpotent maps on R² with composition zero
Connect composition to matrix multiplication of the representing matrices

bank.q: State and prove Sylvester's law of nullity: for linear maps S: U → V and T: V → W with U finite-dimensional, rank(T ∘ S) ≥ rank T + rank S − dim V.
outline: Restrict T to Range S and apply rank-nullity there
ker(T restricted to Range S) = Range S ∩ ker T
Use dim(Range S ∩ ker T) ≤ nullity T
Rearrange to obtain the inequality
Give the matrix version rank(AB) ≥ rank A + rank B − n

bank.q: Let D: P₃ → P₃ be the differentiation map D(p) = p′. Write its matrix in the basis {1, x, x², x³}, find its kernel and range, decide whether D is invertible, and explain what the rank-nullity theorem says here.
outline: Columns are images of 1, x, x², x³: 0, 1, 2x, 3x²
Matrix is nilpotent with zeros on and above a shifted diagonal
ker D = constants, nullity 1; Range D = P₂, rank 3
4 = 3 + 1 confirms the theorem
D is not invertible and the matrix is singular; D⁴ = 0

bank.q: Show that isomorphism is an equivalence relation on vector spaces, that a linear map carries a basis of V to a spanning set of Range T, and explain why the dual space V* is isomorphic to V but is not the same space.
outline: Reflexive: identity map; symmetric: inverse of an isomorphism is linear; transitive: composition of isomorphisms
Images of a basis span the range; drop dependent vectors to get a basis of the range
dim V* = dim V, so V* ≅ V for finite dimension
An isomorphism V → V* needs a chosen basis unless an inner product is given; elements are functionals, not vectors

bank.q: Two matrices represent the same linear operator in different bases exactly when they are similar. Prove this, and use it to argue that rank, nullity, determinant, trace and characteristic polynomial are basis-independent.
outline: If B and A represent T in bases B and C, then B = P⁻¹AP with P the change-of-basis matrix
Conversely, given B = P⁻¹AP, read P as a change of basis and recover T
Similar matrices have equal rank (P and P⁻¹ invertible) and equal determinant and trace
Characteristic polynomial: det(P⁻¹AP − λI) = det(P⁻¹(A − λI)P) = det(A − λI)

glossary.def: A set with addition and scalar multiplication over a field F satisfying the usual eight axioms.
A non-empty subset of a vector space closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
A linearly independent set that spans the space; every vector then has a unique coordinate representation.
The number of vectors in any basis of a finite-dimensional space.
A function between vector spaces preserving addition and scalar multiplication.
The map sending every vector to 0; it is linear and its kernel is the whole space.
I(v) = v for all v; it is linear and invertible.
The set of vectors mapped to zero by a linear map; a subspace of the domain.
The set of all outputs of a linear map; a subspace of the codomain.
The dimension of the kernel.
The dimension of the range.
Distinct inputs give distinct outputs; for linear maps this means the kernel is {0}.
Every vector of the codomain is hit by the map; equivalently the range equals the codomain.
The column of scalars giving a vector as a combination of a chosen basis.
The array whose j-th column is the coordinate vector of the image of the j-th basis vector.
The invertible matrix P that converts old coordinates to new coordinates.
Matrices A and B with B = P⁻¹AP for some invertible P.
A bijective linear map; its inverse is automatically linear.
An invertible linear map between two vector spaces.
Spaces for which some isomorphism exists; over a fixed field this happens exactly when the dimensions agree.
A linear map from a vector space to its field of scalars.
The vector space of all linear functionals on V, denoted V*, with pointwise operations.
The basis of V* dual to a basis of V, defined by fⁱ(vⱼ) = 1 if i = j and 0 otherwise.
The set of functionals that vanish on every vector of a given subspace.
An operator T with Tⁿ = 0 for some positive integer n, such as differentiation on polynomials of bounded degree.
The dimension of its column space, which equals the dimension of its row space.
